original_question: Does the combinatorial 3-polytope FFS3 admit a decomposable geometric realization, where decomposable means representable as a Minkowski sum of two convex bodies that are not similar to one another? Equivalently, is every geometric realization of FFS3 indecomposable?
target_in_paper: Section 4, "Is FFS3 Polytope Decomposable?": the specific conjectural statement that the combinatorial polytope FFS3 has no decomposable geometric realisation. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper: it correctly targets the FFS3 problem in Section 4, correctly treats FFS3 as a combinatorial 3-polytope, and correctly frames the issue as whether there exists a decomposable geometric realisation, using the paper’s Minkowski-sum notion of decomposability. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))
missing_details: A fully stand-alone version should say that a "geometric realization" means a convex 3-polytope in Euclidean 3-space whose combinatorial type (equivalently here, the graph referred to in the paper) is FFS3; the paper identifies FFS3 via the graph shown in Figure 1 rather than by a verbal graph description. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))

The paper gives the similarity notion explicitly: two polytopes are similar if one can be obtained from the other by a dilation and a translation. Your draft uses "not similar" correctly in spirit, but omits this exact definition. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))

The official formulation in the paper is one-sided and conjectural: "It is conjectured that this polytope has no decomposable geometric realisation." A paper-faithful rewrite should track that wording rather than broaden the task. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))

The nearby context says this is the only remaining unresolved case among 3-polytopes with up to 16 edges, and that resolving FFS3 settles the 16-edge case; this is useful scope-setting context, even though it need not be built into the question itself. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))

The section immediately goes on to mention a broader algorithmic challenge for testing decomposability, but that is a separate suggestion and should not be folded into the refined question. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))
refined_question: Let FFS3 denote the combinatorial 3-polytope identified by the graph in Figure 1 of the paper. Is it true that no convex 3-polytope P ⊂ R^3 with combinatorial type FFS3 is decomposable, where decomposable means that P can be written as a Minkowski sum P = A + B of two dissimilar convex bodies, and two polytopes are called similar if one is obtained from the other by a dilation and a translation? ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))
justification: This rewrite stays as close as possible to the paper’s actual intent. The introduction says Section 4 concerns a polytope whose decomposability or indecomposability is hard to determine, and Section 4 then defines decomposable/similar, identifies FFS3 as the only unresolved case in the stated classification program, and records the exact conjectural target: FFS3 has no decomposable geometric realisation. Because the paper does not formulate an equivalence theorem here, and because the subsequent algorithmic challenge is presented as a separate broader direction, the refined question should remain narrowly focused on the existence of a decomposable geometric realisation of FFS3. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))
